rv.q: It’s the best thing writer-director Alexander Zeldin, 41, has done, which is saying something. His previous plays – about zero-hours workers (Beyond Caring); people living in temporary accommodation (Love); and regulars at a community kitchen (Faith, Hope and Charity) – comprise a damning dossier about society’s most vulnerable.
It is gruelling, intense and true, with darkly sublime performances from actors playing the residents.
This is a singular, compassionate piece of work.
It's shamelessly emotionally manipulative in places, with a clanging last note.
Alexander Zeldin’s evocation of end-of-life care is meticulous and hard to watch
Its tender truthfulness makes Care a great play.
And yet it never feels too long.
It 's the sort of role which should give every one of us, renewed respect and admiration for the nursing profession and those who commit their lives to it.
Care is a great theatrical achievement just for its attempts to plumb the subconscious of the elderly, rather than treating them merely as objects of sympathy.

Alexander Zeldin’s CARE, first seen in France in 2022, is certainly a very bleak affair. A friend has just asked me if I enjoyed it, and, to be frank, it is not the sort of play one can enjoy or be entertained by. Having said that, it is compulsive almost hypnotic in all of its 125 minutes. It is also superbly acted by all concerned.
Summarised in that way, the play might sound simplistic or even banal; in fact, it is a profound and expert dramatic achievement.

cn.t: Zeldin's meticulous portrayal of end-of-life care proves devastating and hard to watch, yet ultimately thoughtful and uplifting. Critics praise its tender truthfulness while noting emotional manipulation in places.
